newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan fighting swirls north of Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Afghan fighting swirls north of Kabul.

text.p: Fighting swirled north of Kabul on Tuesday, with forces loyal to former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood pressing hard to recapture the Afghan capital, while Taleban militia regained ground elsewhere, witnesses said.
Fighting erupted around midday in the small market town of Qara Bagh, which sits astride the main highway running north from Kabul about 50 km (30 miles) outside the capital.

An hour earlier reporters who had been told the town was in the hands of Masood's forces were startled to find a white flag fluttering above the marketplace -- used by the ultra-conservative Islamic Taleban to mark their territory and to signify their purity.
"We are Taleban and we welcome you," Mohamed Ismail, an elderly, bearded local cleric, told the reporters.
"This town is now completely secure under Taleban. There is no fear of attack. Everyone here believes in the Koran. All we want now is peace."
Masood was military chief under the government of Afghan President Burhanuddin Rabbani, which was driven from Kabul by the Taleban.
Like many towns north of Kabul, Qara Bagh and its citizens have had to be supple in serving a rapidly shifting series of masters.

Masood's troops had retaken the town just two days ago but neglected to garrison it and local residents said the Taleban slipped into the southern part on Monday and took the rest overnight on Tuesday, under cover of darkness and without a fight.
Jeeps, trucks and buses filled with Masood's soldiers streamed towards Qara Bagh from Jabal os-Siraj in the early afternoon, eager to reclaim lost ground.

The soldiers stopped reporters trying to re-enter Qara Bagh about ten km (six miles) north of the town where the main highway forks northeast towards the military airfield at Bagram -- another site of fighting on Tuesday.

The sound of heavy artillery and what seemed to be aircraft bombs rumbled menacingly over the plains south of Jabal os-Siraj at midday, indicating strong fighting in that vicinity -- about 90 km (60 miles) north of Kabul.

Aid workers in the town of Charikar 10 km (six miles) to the south saw an aircraft circling at about the same time and said anti-aircraft guns around the town let loose a hail of fire but failed to bring it down.

Charikar, held by Masood's forces, was bombed on Monday afternoon by an unknown aircraft, presumably flying in support of Taleban forces. Nine persons were killed and six were wounded, witnesses said.
Elsewhere, Masood's sources said they were closing in on Sarobi on the main highway about 70 km (45 miles) east of Kabul.
Along the road to Bagram at a hamlet called Rabat, the commander of the last non-Taleban checkpoint said he was sickened by the country's recent return to war.
"Our best young men are being killed because of this fighting and there's no point to it," the commander -- who refused to be identified -- stammered as he fought back tears of frustration and rage.
"This is all the work of America. It makes the factions fight among themselves. Why should we fight and die? We are all Moslems. We should be at peace with one another."

Many supporters of Rabbani and apolitical Afghans alike believe the United States and Pakistan, motivated by an interest in containing the influence of Iran and former Soviet states, have conspired to support the startling rise to power of the Taleban.
After retreating from Kabul in late September forces under Masood have been fighting their way back towards the capital and making a considerable effort to recapture the airfield at Bagram.
On Monday a senior commander loyal to Masood told reporters his men held the military base except for the southern tip of the main runway while Taleban held the town itself.
